Standard: Engine components are free of damaging vibration, damaging resonance conditions, or other damaging DR, regardless of propulsion system excitation source, when operated, at all engine-rotational speeds and thrust or power settings under installed or uninstalled steady state and transient conditions, at maximum allowable field imbalance of the engine rotor systems, IAW 7.3.1 for the stated life documented in engine technical data. a. Maximum vibratory stress is below minimum Goodman allowable limits for the following cyclic endurance capability: 1. Titanium 109 cycles. 2. Other Metallic Materials 107 cycles. 3. Composite or Other Materials 3 X 107 cycles. Maximum vibratory stress for flow-path components and components subject to high variability or uncertainty in forcing, dynamic characteristics, coupling, or damping does not exceed 60% of the Goodman limit (40% margin). Such components comprise rotating components, rotating assemblies, rotating seals, shafts, airfoils (e.g., blades, vanes, stators, nozzles), struts, fuel nozzles, and control system probes that protrude into the turbomachinery flow path (e.g., T2 sensor). Reduced vibratory stress margin for other components will be justified. b. Self-excited vibrations such as flutter, separated flow vibration, or other non-integral vibrations do not occur within the operating range of the engine. Any required operation or installation limits are defined. Method of Compliance: Prior to entering flight test, verify the standard by the following method(s): Examination.
(1) Operating limits to prevent damaging response or component failure are defined in engine technical data.
(2) Installation requirements to prevent damaging response or component failure are defined in the ICD. Analysis.
  (1) Analysis is accomplished to determine vibratory characteristics of engine components and assemblies (e.g., frequencies, mode shapes, damping, coupling, mistuning, coincidence). Analysis is calibrated to component, rig, and engine test results. Models are used to evaluate sensitivity to influence parameters (boundary conditions, geometry, manufacturing, operating conditions). Campbell diagrams are prepared to verify margin to potential resonances (e.g. low-order crossings, upstream and downstream counts) particularly at sustained power operating ranges. Models are used to guide instrumentation layout for testing. Model quality is assessed using HCF Protocol described in JSSG-2007, Appendix A, Verification section, Component Vibrations paragraph.
  (2) Goodman diagrams, with maximum and minimum stress truncated to yield strength, are prepared using calibrated models and test results. Models and test results are used to project maximum responses throughout the operating range and envelope.
  (3) Analysis of rig and engine test results are conducted to determine operating limits for self-excited vibrations and to verify that responses do not occur in the engine operating range. Test.
    (1) Lab test: Bench and rig tests are accomplished to determine component and assembly vibratory characteristics (e.g. frequencies, mode shapes, damping, coupling, mistuning, coincidence), to determine peak vibratory response, and to inform instrumentation application for subsequent engine tests. Multiple components and assemblies are tested to determine variability across a range of influence parameters.
    (2) Lab test: Instrumented core and engine tests are conducted in sea-level and altitude test cells using production configuration hardware and control schedules. Aeromechanical stress surveys are accomplished to verify vibratory stresses and stability margins, including flutter. Test conditions for aeromechanical tests include exposure to a range of influence parameters (e.g., rotor imbalance, off-nominal vane schedules, air vehicle inlet conditions, engine inlet total pressure and total temperature, expected inlet distortion and separation, accessory loads, stalls, bleed, multiple engines) per the HCF Protocol described in JSSG-2007, Appendix A, Verification section, Component Vibrations paragraph to verify robustness to expected variation, and also aerodynamic and aeromechanical factors that might induce or influence flutter.
    (3) Lab test: Full engine durability test or AMT/ASMET is conducted in a ground-based sea level test cell and includes HCF stairsteps in 50-60 RPM increments and dwell times IAW JSSG- 2007, Appendix A, Verification section, Endurance Tests paragraph.
    (4) Ground test: Ground test with an instrumented engine is conducted using production configuration hardware and control schedules, and production inlet configuration to verify installed vibratory and flutter response. Static crosswind conditions are included in the evaluation. Prior to entering operational test/operations, verify the standard by the above and following method(s): Test.
    (5) Flight test: Flight test with an instrumented engine is conducted using production configuration hardware and control schedules, and production inlet configuration to verify installed vibratory and flutter response.
